utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, we were left in the position that you were expressing a preference for one witness to be dealt with first this afternoon. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I had to think for a moment. I'm sorry. Yes. Mr. Grubisic's examination, if the Chamber is so minded, it would be very helpful, so he can return to give mass. And we also submitted, so the Chamber is aware, another issue with a witness having a problem for deadlines next week, and I've transmitted it through the appropriate channels. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, I would like to address you for only two minutes, in connection with something that is becoming a cause of concern. The Defence understands that the testimony of witnesses before this Tribunal is an honour and a privilege for each witness. Unfortunately, we are now in a situation where the witnesses are at the disposal of the Trial Chamber and all of us here in the courtroom, at those times when they have nothing more important to do. However, the most important job of a witness who has agreed to testify before this Tribunal is to testify. Practically every day a witness is expressing his or her preferences as to what days they can come and testify, or for how long they can stay. One witness can testify on Friday, another on Monday or Thursday or Friday, in accordance with their wishes. The witness Paul Davies started his testimony and had to interrupt because Mrs. Alajbeg had only two days. The same situation is recurring now. The same witness will testify now, and he will be cross-examined for an hour or two. He will be followed by Samardzic but tomorrow Djelo Jusic will begin he has to leave on Monday. It is simply impossible to work this day. Do these people want to testify or not? If they do, they have to set aside sufficient time to testify before this Chamber. We can understand exceptional situations, but out of eight witnesses, at least five had had special witnesses [as interpreted] as to when they can testify or not. They have to testify when the Trial Chamber so orders and not when they have nothing better to do. We ask the Chamber to take this into account because we think it will be very difficult to proceed in this manner. Look at the witness Pringle, for example, a crucial witness. Yesterday we were told that he can testify for only two days, on the 29th and the 30th, and he is witnessing as to command and control, which is a key area. What are we to do? He's here for only two days. If we don't complete our examination, then the entire schedule would be in disarray, we will be under pressure to speed up. He will -- or he will have to come back, and more costs will be incurred. The Prosecutor has to plan her time. This is the fourth time we have been given a revised schedule. We know that there are objective problems. We accept that and we are trying to be cooperative, but this kind of organisation will simply lead us into an impossible situation. I have three pieces of paper before me telling when which witness will be able to testify. It's up to the Chamber to determine that. The primary obligation of these witnesses should be the Tribunal, and only then should it be mass or something else. And I ask that the Prosecutor's office have their attention drawn to this. We are prepared to be flexible, but this cannot become the rule. Thank you, Your Honour, and I apologise for taking so much time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think the only thing with which I can concur from this last exchange is that it is indeed for most people truly an honour and a privilege to come. Most of the persons involved are professionals, many of them are professionals, like ourselves. Many have obligations which they have set aside in order to come. I'm sure I don't have to remind the Chamber that for us even to start, we had to accommodate the schedule of General Strugar as opposed to the schedule of the Chamber, which had directed that he be returned to the Tribunal, and accordingly, I think these inconveniences are relatively, if not minor, then at least respectful of the obligation to be before the Tribunal. We inform the Chamber, as the Chamber requested. We are not able to ask people to set aside their lives completely. We cannot compel people to come. And if there is a way that we can accommodate, within the Chamber's, of course, understanding and sound discretion, then it is our job to make sure, as the Chamber directed us to do, to let you know. In the main, on relatively short notice, because of the back and forth with scheduling, and because of the serious delays work by the Defence in just appearing for trial upon order, we have had to say -- change dates a number of times. Things such as the illness of the witness are unforeseeable, and I don't think that there's any need to make an excuse for this type of request. If the Chamber accepts as valid and understands, which I'm sure it does, given the nature of this Tribunal as opposed to a domestic court, where there is more control and travel is not necessarily involved, then I think that the record would speak for itself. We have always tried, through the very good offices of the Victims and Witness Unit, and a special assignment of an investigative staff member, to line up witnesses so that it is orderly. When issues come, if, for example, a cross-examination, rightly or wrongly, takes more time than is anticipated, or an issue arises, we have no option except to ask for an interruption. It is not optimal, but that's what happens. And the Chamber's own schedule oftentimes requires that we have to adjust things. I do not see this as a harmful pattern. It is certainly not something that is devised by any witness with any malice. But because we are asking people to come when they don't have to, and because they want to come, we attempt to accommodate, and I'm sure when the Defence starts its case and similar requests are made, we'll have to revisit it as well, and I think the Prosecution has always expressed its willingness, irrespective of whatever delays are incurred by the Defence, to rise to the occasion. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It appears to the Chamber that there is a good deal of merit in what both counsel have put. We well understand that, from the point of view of the Defence counsel, the ability to know where to focus their preparation for cross-examination and the ability to conduct in one continuous session a cross-examination is highly desirable and would be something that they would normally expect should occur. We also fully appreciate, as Ms. Somers has put, that the conduct of this hearing to date has suffered some significant interruptions which have put out of the planned order a great deal to do with the times when witnesses had planned to be here and has affected their availability. We would also add that, with one or two of the witnesses, the length of time spent in cross-examination has also affected the programme. It appears that it is not necessary at the moment to make any further observations about these matters. It is our hope and expectation that we will very shortly be able to get back into a substantially normal pattern, when a witness will come, give the evidence the witness seeks to give, will be cross-examined, and will go, and we will then move to the next witness in an orderly manner. At the moment, we are disrupted in that order, and that will -- while it will require added flexibility on the part of all counsel, and on the part of the Chamber, it is necessary and essential at the present time to put up with that. The steps that have been taken and the measures that are in place appear to us to be ones that will give to Defence counsel reasonable notice in the circumstances of the witnesses they can expect to be called in the next day or two or three days, and against the background of their normal thorough preparation for the case, that should enable them to cope with the exigencies of cross-examination as they arise. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. While we fully sympathise, Mr. Petrovic, with your concern, I think in this case we just must let the present circumstances work their way out, so that hopefully we can get back to a normal pattern. I see nothing at the moment about what is proposed which would warrant any special action on the part of the Chamber at the present time. But certainly, we are anxious, as you are, that the matters should get back to a more normal pattern. Well, if the witness, then, could be called. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. If I could just remind you of the affirmation that you took at the commencement of your evidence, which is still operative. Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Grubisic. I'm Vladimir Petrovic, an attorney from Belgrade, counsel for General Strugar, and I will put some questions to you in connection with your testimony of yesterday before this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us that at the time we were discussing, in the autumn of 1991, you were living in Celestina Medovica Street number 4; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Before we continue, let me just ask you that, in view of the fact that you understand me without waiting for an interpretation, please leave a pause between my question and your answer, so that others who do not understand our language can hear the interpretation and follow what we are saying. So please make a brief pause after my question so that the interpretation can finish. Celestina Medovica Street, in what part of Dubrovnik is that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you enter from the Pile gate, it's the first street on the left, as you go towards the town from the Pile gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it the street that has residential buildings on one side and the Franciscan monastery on the other?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how wide that street is?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two metres, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: It's one of those narrow Dubrovnik streets?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In which building were you living in 1991? And maybe you still reside there today. What kind of building is it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the first building after Prijeko Street, the first entrance on the right and that's where my cellar is where we took shelter. The second door is the entrance to my house, or rather, it's not my house; it belongs to the church. But two priests live there. The first one was on the first floor, and the ground floor, and I myself lived on the second floor. I was the second priest. I had about 35 square metres of residential space.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is this building often referred to as the priest's house in Dubrovnik? Is that what it's called?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are quite a few church-owned buildings in Dubrovnik, which were confiscated after World War II, but a few houses were left for priests to live in. However -- or rather, the street in Celestina Medovica Street number 4, that's one of those buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What is there at number 6 and number 8 in the same street?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right next door to my house is the side entrance to the convent of the Zigurate nuns, but they actually used the Zigurate entrance. And then there's a postman's house, Mico Djenovic [phoen]. Further on, at the next house number, which is what you asked me, no one lives there. It belongs to someone who used to live in Belgrade, but he has relatives who sometimes use that house. And then the Danicic family live at the next house number, and then there's another street, called Ispod Mincete.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Looking towards the Minceta tower, you described to us the right-hand side of the street, Celestina Medovica Street. Can you briefly now describe the left-hand side of this street, from Prijeko upwards.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Prijeko upwards, from the start of the street to the top, it's all the Franciscan monastery. First there's the church, then the old pharmacy, then the monastery. Opposite my door is an auxiliary entrance to the monastery. Then there's the monastery garden. So all the way up to the Minceta tower, this whole complex belongs to the Franciscan monastery and no one lives there except the Franciscans.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is there a garden there? Is there a fence?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the top there's a playing field, or rather, a playground, where children play, under the Minceta tower, and then in the garden there is a building that was once used for making candles, but it burnt down. I don't remember exactly when, but before the war, certainly before the war. This war did not have any influence on that. And in the garden there are oranges, lemons, fruit trees, and when there were more Franciscans there, they also grew vegetables there, but they don't any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How high is the fence, or the wall of this garden?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure, but it's quite tall. I never visited that playground, but I can see from my window that this fence is quite tall, so that when the children are playing in the playground, their ball wouldn't constantly go into the monastery garden.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In that area, the closest walls to where you live are the ones between the Pile gate and the Minceta tower at the corner?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How tall are the city walls between the Pile gate and the Minceta tower?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly, but if we start from the Stradun to my house, there are about 30 steps. If I were to calculate how tall each step was, it would be about 20 centimetres, I think. There are also 30 or 35 steps inside the house leading to my apartment, and when I look out from my window, I'm at the level of the top of the wall leading to the Minceta tower. But then the wall rises as it goes towards the Minceta tower. I don't know how tall the Minceta tower is. Well, I wouldn't be able to respond with any precision, but this is about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So from your window, you can see the wall?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We shall go back to this issue again later. Yesterday you mentioned Priest Milan Majic, and you also said that before the 1st of October, you received an invitation from him. Did I understand properly your answer?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise. In order for me not to be confused, you are referring to the 1st of October?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. Given the differences between our two languages, I will try to pose questions in a way that you will be able to understand. Therefore, was it before the 1st of October, 1991 he got in touch with you? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were best of friends. I lost him. He died of cancer two years ago. We used to talk on the phone almost every day. He called me a few days before that and said that the shelling of Zupa had already started, and also firing. He asked me, and I also advised him to come over to me to spend a few days at my place. He did come before the 1st of October to my place, and he was the one who stayed longest in my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did Priest Majic tell you what the fighting was about, who was fighting who?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no fighting at all, because there was no one to fight. That was simply shelling. Shells were falling on Brgat and Zupa. And one could hear from above Ivanica light machine-guns and other small arms being fired. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All of that was happening in late September, if I understand you correctly.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps ask Priest Majic were Croatian policemen or soldiers in Brgat, the defenders, or you didn't ask him that at all?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not ask him, but probably if there were any some self-organised local residents, but for sure there was no police or army there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you go there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went there very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you go there in September?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you -- forgive me. I hear you and then I start talking again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I made the same mistake, so I hope the Chamber will have understanding for both of us. So were you there in September?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was there several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you go there while the shelling was in progress?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once, I can't remember exactly when, but I believe that it was either in late September or early October, most probably already after Dubrovnik had been -- the transmitter on the Srdj had been demolished. We didn't have any electrical power. We went up there. We were rather naive, because the church was hit by four or five shells. We brought with us some tarpaulin in order to cover the church. When we arrived at his house, and when we saw that a shell had fallen --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grubisic --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please, you're answering my questions. The Prosecutor asked what they believe is important, and I am going to ask you the questions that I believe are of importance for my defence. So my question is whether, at the time that you were there, you did not see any defenders there.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not a single defender.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any JNA soldiers perhaps there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. But above the hill, the Postranje, there was fire coming from some machine-guns. Therefore, we had to rush and escape, due to which he wasn't able to bring any basic belongings that he would need for survival.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did your niece come to stay with you? Was that before the 1st of October?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many days before the 1st of October? Two or three, four days?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, but for sure she did come at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And she told you that she had left Mlini because she couldn't sleep because of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was constant firing coming from the hills, and also there was shelling and, and due to that, they had to leave their homes. But they reckoned and they thought that they could go back quickly and that it was something that was only temporary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. If I understood you properly yesterday, those families stayed with you for approximately one month, so they spent the month of October with you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The women and the children, once the blockade was broken through and the Libertas convoy and other ships started taking women and children away, it was then when my niece and Mioc's wife and children set off for Split, whereas we, the men, and the Serb woman Slavka Tomovic and her husband, remained in my house. We probably stayed there for about one month.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned several people. You just mentioned Serbs by their nationality, not others. What do you think that is important? Why didn't you say that Marija Lemo was Croat? Why do you always emphasise that the Tomovic's were the Serbs? Why was that important? Human beings are human beings. They fled their places of residence, regardless of the fact whether they were Serbs or Croats.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was necessary to underlie that specifically in order to demonstrate that there was no interethnic conflict, especially not an interreligious conflict, and that I, in my capacity of a priest, by abiding by the command "Love thy Neighbour," and that one should be obliged to help other people, and therefore provide shelter not only for their relatives but also for the Croats and Serbs as well. That is why I thought it was necessary to stress that particularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't the fathers and the husbands leave with their families towards Split? Why did they stay behind in your flat? Why they didn't join their wives and children?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, our intention was not to abandon Dubrovnik and that no one should leave Dubrovnik, especially not males and those who were fit for defence, should it become necessary. But a city without inhabitants, without people who live there, is a dead town. For that reason, the men stayed behind in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the men did not leave in order to defend the city?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said. I'm sorry. They did not have any means with which to defend the city. Maybe I didn't put it properly. Perhaps they just wanted to render moral support for as many people to remain in the city as possible. Our bishop also appealed to people to stay behind. But I believe that it is better if we spare the women and the children the hell and to send them away once it became possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did Vinko Mioc, if he wanted, was he able to join his wife Angela and leave?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he could have left, but, as far as I know - or at least those were the rumours. I wasn't in Gruz at the time - they had to go to Zelenika. Every ship had to go to Zelenika for inspection. And it was dangerous for men who were fit of being captured and taken away to an undisclosed location. Probably there was some fear, and that is why he didn't leave, but he could have left.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So not a single adult male was forbidden to leave the city; is that what you are saying in this testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was a recommendation for people to stay in the city, not to leave it. But I cannot answer your question whether anyone was involved in the defence or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know any person who had left?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some people managed to squeeze out, and they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who was controlling who was boarding the ships, either in Gruz or the Old Town harbour?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. There was no boarding the ship in the Old Town, only in Gruz, but I never went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You say that some people managed to squeeze out or smuggle themselves out. Who were they hiding from so that they had to resort to this method?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me whether anyone had left. I told you: Probably yes. I cannot tell you who they were hiding from.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean, they smuggled themselves out? With reference to whom?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let me try to clarify. Did they sneak out vis-a-vis the Croatian authority or vis-a-vis the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe both, because they were afraid and they wished to avoid being captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Although there was no electric power, you received news over the radio. You had a transistor or something similar that you were able to listen to and hear what was happening in Dubrovnik and in Croatia and further afield?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We had a transistor radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you listen to the news on that transistor radio? I presume you did, given the situation that you were in.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear on the news that general mobilisation was called in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were called up here and there. We heard it on the news, to go and defend our homeland, which was unjustifiably attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were the people from Dubrovnik called up?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were in a sort of a concentration camp, surrounded from all sides, without food, without anything. So who was really going to call up anyone to go and defend something with their bare hands? So my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You also said yesterday that two Tomovics from this Serbian family, as you say, went and joined the HVO. Do you know what the HVO is?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's an abbreviation for the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is that a military formation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a military person, so please don't ask me this kind of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was that a citizens' association? Was that a voluntary company, a club? What?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the very name, you can see that it says it's the Croatian Defence Council, and I beg of you not to insist upon this issue any more, because I can only speak about what I have been through personally and what I have seen. As for other questions, you may as well ask them, but I don't believe that it is my duty to answer that sort of question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grubisic, in your statement, in response to the questions of my learned colleague Weiner you mentioned a military formation, the HVO. The Rules of this Tribunal, which you may not know, but I will tell you, allow me to ask the question about what you mentioned yesterday in your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. I don't believe it's counsel's duty or obligation to be discussing the Rules of this Tribunal with the witness. If he has -- if he feels that there is an issue, I think he should notify the Bench and let the Bench advise the witness as to the Rules. Further, I believe the witness is indicating he does not know anything about the HVO, so it would also be asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If I could indicate, Don Grubisic, that it is appropriate for you to answer questions that are put to you, if you do know the answer. If you do not know the answer, just say that and counsel will move on to the next question. If you would continue, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was the HVO an armed military organisation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the Croatian army is?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess the army that defends its country, just like any other army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what is the National Guard Corps?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what MUP is?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's the police, the Ministry of the Interior. That's what it's supposed to mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what HOS is, HOS?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what is the 116th Brigade of the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Nojko Marinovic is?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard of him. I don't know him personally, but I did hear that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you had heard about him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he was in the JNA -- had been in the JNA, and that later he joined the Croatian Army. He was a sort of a commander, but I can't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know that Mr. Marinovic was in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know that Mr. Marinovic was the commander of the defence of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was some stories about that that I heard on the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what Marinovic commanded in Dubrovnik, given your statement that in Dubrovnik you had never seen any soldiers or other armed people except for the policemen armed with small arms?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object. I object. May I speak, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Weiner. I didn't have you in my sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm short, but I didn't think I was that short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No. I had a very focussed look in another direction. Height was not an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The statement here is a direct misquotation of the evidence. Our evidence of this witness has been that there has been no troops, no artillery, no military presence in the Old Town of Dubrovnik. The Old Town of Dubrovnik, as the testimony has come through from other witnesses, is part of a larger municipality of Dubrovnik. And he has used a confusing question to try and indicate that there were troops, and that yesterday he indicated that there were no troops in the Old Town of Dubrovnik, and now he's saying that he is aware that there was a military commander of the municipality of Dubrovnik. And I think his questions should be far more specific, because we're dealing with two different areas. I have no objection to him asking questions in that area, but those are not fair questions and they're confusing questions and I feel trying to confuse the panel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I think there was a distinction in the evidence between the greater or larger municipality of Dubrovnik and the Old Town of Dubrovnik, and you may keep that in mind as you frame your questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understood yesterday's testimony very well. My question was more general. Because this witness moved about outside the boundaries of the Old Town. So it's quite clear that he can answer my question and that it's fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think Mr. Grubisic made clear that you were talking not just about the Old Town but the larger municipality when you question about Dubrovnik it will be easier for the witness then to deal with your question and answer it for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the questions are already limited to the area that the witness visited, that is, the Old Town, Gruz, Lapad, so that anything I ask, if it's not clear to the witness, let me clarify it now. When I say "Dubrovnik," I'm referring to Gruz, Lapad, Babin Kuk, the town, not the municipality, but the town. When I'm asking about the Old Town, I will of course specify this, but I will probably not go into that at all, because my learned friend asked about that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. I think that helps me, and I believe it may help the witness as well. But I see Mr. Weiner on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I was just going to add that we've already been discussing Brgat, which is far outside the Old Town. It's another village, or a community, a distance away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you could move on with your questions, Mr. Petrovic. You've made clear what you're intending by them, and I'm sure the witness has understood what you've said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I ask you to bear with me for a moment so I can recall where I stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The last question I put to you concerned Nojko Marinovic. You told me that you knew that he was a commander or something like that. Can you tell me what he was commander of, to avoid any misunderstanding? So I'm not asking you whether he was a commander in the Old Town or outside the Old Town, but what was your understanding of the role of Mr. Marinovic? What do you know about it? At the time, of course, in October, November, and December 1991. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I feel that it is my duty to answer your questions, and as Mr. Weiner said, yesterday I talked only about what I had experienced in the Old Town. I didn't go about much further afield, for reasons of security, safety. But as for your question, Mr. Nojko Marinovic was later on -- well, later on, some sort of defence was set up, as far as the town was concerned. Because, as far as I know, on Srdj there were 10, 15, or 20 soldiers who were defending the town and who, on the 6th of December, held their positions heroically, resisting the attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What were they armed with? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. I apologise for rushing in with my reply, without waiting for the interpretation. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were they members of the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Probably they were, the defenders. They were not an army; they were defenders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please clarify what "defenders" are and what the difference is between defenders and the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the word "defender" shows that they are defending themselves from something or someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What, then, is the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not a military expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, this is not a military question; it's a question of general education, to which anyone can reply.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, every nation, if you insist, has an army, and so Croatia also should have its army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did Croatia have its own army in December 1991 in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How do you know this, when you say that you did not leave the Old Town or that you did so very rarely?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no soldiers about. People would have known about this. Dubrovnik is a small town. Everybody knows what other people are doing. They know what they're having for dinner. You wouldn't be able to conceal an army there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That's just what I'm -- why I'm putting you this question, because many of your fellow citizens say they were members of the Croatian Army and that they defended the town of Dubrovnik heroically. How is it possible that none of your parishioners or neighbours or friends ever said to you that there were Croatian soldiers in the town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assert categorically that there were no Croatian soldiers in the Old Town. As I said, as far as I know, there were some 20 or so defenders on Srdj.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that on the 1st of October the power and water were cut off. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: After that, you told us that on the 5th of October you went to the Lero Hotel. Where did you go? What route did you take? What route did you take on your way back, and when did the attack begin?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don Milan and I set out because one of his parishioners was seriously ill. We went from the Old Town towards the old hospital, through Boninovo towards Gospino Polje, and so we arrived at the Lero hotel. When he had performed the duty for which he had gone there, the shooting began. On our way back through Gospino Polje, some hundred metres away from Hotel Lero, a man gave us a lift in his car, and we didn't go by way of Boninovo but we went towards the post office, on Ilijina Glavica. We got out of the car there, and the shooting was very intense by then. We took a street that we call Busovina. I don't know if that's its official name, but we called it that. We took that street to Hotel Imperial. Then we went behind the Atlas building, at Pile, and so reached the entrance to the Old Town. We saw that the gate was closed. And as I described yesterday, we came in through a small side door, because in the big gate there is a small door. And we fled to my cellar. When the shelling stopped, we saw that the Rupe museum building had been hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please limit yourself to answering my question, to avoid wasting time. Are there any trees around the post office at Glavica? Is there a park, a wood?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front of the post office, there are some pine trees or cypresses, in front of the post office, toward the road. And between the pavement and the road, there are flowers, flower beds.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the cellar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the shelling stopped. But truth to tell, I'm not sure. It was some 13 or 14 years ago, so that's a question I find very difficult to answer, because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, can you help me whether it was an hour, two, three, 15 minutes, the whole day? Approximately. I'm not asking for a precise time.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was not all day. It started in the afternoon. But I can't tell you how long we were there. Please don't insist, because I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What time of day was it when the shelling started?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the afternoon, about 3.00 or 4.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You remember when the shelling started, but you don't remember how long you spent in the cellar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know because we went to the Lero Hotel after lunch. We stayed there some 15 or 20 minutes and then went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How long did the journey back take?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some 20 minutes or so. We walked fast, and as I said, we were given a lift for part of the way. It was less than a kilometre. There was a car that happened to be passing by that gave us a lift.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So it was broad daylight when the shelling started?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And at twilight you went out of the cellar, you were already at home or performing your other duties?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For as long as the shelling went on, we stayed in the cellar. As soon as the shelling stopped, I would go to my flat, because the entrance to the cellar and the entrance to the house are only a few metres apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you spend that night in the cellar or did you go home?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't spend any nights in the cellar. Throughout the war, we always slept -- well, not in our beds, but in my apartment, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, whenever the attack -- an attack started, would you rush down to the cellar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On that day, did you go down to the cellar again or was it just on that one occasion, that one time when you came back from the Lero Hotel that you went down to the cellar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was only once, because the shelling, at least as far as the Old Town goes, lasted a short time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And the cellar is in your building, in the building you live in?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I assume it's dark in the cellar.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite dark, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I assume you can't see out from the cellar. Maybe it has no windows at all.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a window. It has a small opening for air, for ventilation, but we always kept the door open.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Open to where?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The door of the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you're sitting in the cellar and looking out the door, what do you see?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All you see is the wall of the Franciscan monastery. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You told me that at Porporela, you had seen some armed men. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said. I said that I had seen two uniformed policemen with automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Can you distinguish an automatic rifle and a semi-automatic rifle, for instance?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had been in the military a long time ago. At the time, those automatic rifles were very old, made in Kragujevac. So an automatic, or a semi-automatic gun, is something that we used to call Parabela. So it resembled that. But I really cannot tell you what is the distinction between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why were they armed with those rifles there at Porporela? Was it not enough for them to have just pistols, which is the normal practice with the police?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I explained that yesterday. This is the entry point to the town, and I believe this was more for giving moral support or for any concrete defence purposes or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that they were there in order to prevent anyone docking there in the town.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what could two policemen prevent, if a destroyer arrived, or any other big ship? I just told you that I think it was just a moral support. They would have fled the place much quicker than you can think.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: They would have fled probably because of the inequality between them and the possible attacker?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So tell me how those dozen men did not flee Srdj, as they were also on an equal -- unequal position as compared to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Number one, he's asking a military question. The witness has just been speculating. Now he's asking a military question. He's never been up on Srdj; there's no testimony about him being up on Srdj or being involved in the military. This is outside the scope of his testimony. And I feel you're asking an opinion for a military expert. It's not for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Petrovic, no need for you to respond. I'd have thought it very obvious the answer of this witness will be: I don't know. I can't help. And that will be the end of this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am satisfied if I get that kind of answer. He could just say, simply: I don't know. Whether the brave defenders of Srdj would have left their position. So I would be happy with his saying: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They did not abandon their position.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they were brave.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were they well armed or were they just brave?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what weapons they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So how do you know that they were brave, if you don't know anything about what was happening up there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spent that day in our cellars, and I said that it was hell. The fact is that they remained up there on Srdj and they did not run away.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: On the 5th of October, was an air raid siren sounded -- or alert sounded in the town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were frequent alerts in the town, and I suppose that was the case on that day too. However, no attack was expected then. Whenever an attack was expected, the alarm was sounded. And I cannot tell you exactly whether it was sounded on that day or whether how long it lasted. I can tell you that on St. Nicholas, which is the 6th of December, the air raid alert was on the whole day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please concentrate on my question only. You said: "When an attack was expected or anticipated". How could you know when to anticipate or expect an attack?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not able to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So why did you say just now: However, this attack was not expected? Were other situations when attacks were expected?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: While you were in the cellar, were you able to know what was going on in the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only if we listened to the radio. But as far as the Old Town is concerned, we could only know if we went out there to see for ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That means the whole time that you were in the cellars, you had no idea and you had no way of knowing what was going on in the town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You couldn't possibly know who was coming into the Old Town or who was coming out of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I already answered this question. How could I have known who was coming in or going out if I was in a cellar?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So how can you know, then, that there was not a single bullet fired in the Old Town, if you had spent days or hours or end in the cellar? How can you know that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, why would anyone shoot inside the Old Town? There was no army there, and the civilians were hiding in cellars because they were afraid. Therefore, I can be 100 per cent sure that there was no shooting. And even if -- or we would have heard if there were any shots fired nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So from your cellar, you could have judged whether anyone was firing inside the town or at the town or beside the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Since you aren't in any way a military expert, how were you able to discern whether anyone was opening fire at several hundred metres away from you? Based on what could you make such a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were about ten people in the cellar at times, and it's quite normal that whenever we heard a shell, although I have some hearing problems, to tell you the truth, but there were other people, and we could have simply concluded. But I adamantly state that there was no shooting and no soldiers in the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Except that you couldn't know what was going on while you were in the shelter.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we were in the shelters, and we had to go there because the town was being shelled, then how can anyone from the Old Town shoot? That is my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear during those three months that anyone fired a shell, a bullet, inside the town or around the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday negotiations. Who was representing Croatia in those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were frequently replaced, so I cannot say exactly who was negotiating on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about that specific day. I'm asking you whether you know who represented Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were different people coming and going. They were not always the same negotiators.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you mention one name?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djuro Kolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you add any more names?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, but I'm not sure, that one of them was Cico Obuljen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what a crisis staff is?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard there was a crisis staff in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that on the radio, that the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik was issuing statements?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who governed the city during those three months of 1991? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what you mean by "who governed the town." I think that Petar Poljanic was the president of the Municipal Assembly at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did he represent the Croatian authorities in the town at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that he was the president of the town, and I believe that a person in such position governs the city. If that is what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did any people come from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, people came from Zagreb. There were foreign observers. It was quite normal that people came to the town from all quarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any of the ministers from the Croatian government or did you hear that any one of them visited the city?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Stipe Mesic maybe visited Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that visit, because he came when the first convoy arrived, and he was at the helm of this convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any other names?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Through the Pile gate, was there always, or is it still now, which is less important, permitted for motor vehicles to enter the town, motorcycles, vans, delivery vans? Are they allowed to pass through the gate into the town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but all the deliveries arrive from the direction of Ploce. This gate is reserved for emergencies only, for instance, for an ambulance. Otherwise, it is forbidden for any motor vehicles to enter the town from Pile.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could a small van, a small lorry, pass -- or come into the town, whether from Pile or from Ploce?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me, I think that this would be the right time for us to take a break, if you agree. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that indication, Mr. Petrovic. I think it's a good opportunity now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just before you continue, Mr. Petrovic, could I indicate that, as foreshadowed yesterday, it will not be convenient for the Trial Chamber to resume for the third session this afternoon, so that we will break at some time between a quarter past and half past 5.00, and that will be the end of the hearing time this afternoon. Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will do my utmost to complete my cross-examination by that time, if not before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grubisic, I would now like to focus on the 6th of December. Tell me, please: When, in your recollection, did the attack of the 6th of December begin? And please be as brief as possible, so that you can get away tomorrow. Because, as you see, our sitting today will be shorter. So when, in your recollection, did the attack begin?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At about 5.30 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did you see shells landing in the vicinity of the Dubrovnik Cafe?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is that at around 5.30 or 6.00 a.m.? Was it then that you saw shells landing around the Dubrovnik Cafe, near the Pile gate?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, the Dubrovnik Cafe. Sorry. I didn't understand. Yes. At that point, we got up, and I saw that the Imperial Hotel had been hit. That's what I can see from my window. And I saw that the Dubrovnik Cafe had been hit. And I saw that looking over the walls from my room.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: You said yesterday that the Dubrovnik Cafe is some 10 or 15 metres away from the Pile gate; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And Pile is the entrance to the Old Town, the Pile gate, that is, from the west; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please explain to me how you could have seen from your window something that is ten metres away from the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't see the cafe itself. I have a direct view of the Imperial Hotel over the city walls but not the cafe itself. However, when the shell landed, I saw the smoke rising from just behind the walls, and that was when the cafe was hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you assumed that Dubrovnik Cafe had been hit?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, I assumed it. And on the next day, I was able to ascertain that for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you tell us yesterday that you assumed that the Dubrovnik Cafe had been hit? You told the Chamber that you saw the Dubrovnik Cafe being hit.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have just told you: I did see the smoke rising after the shell landed. If I use the words that you have quoted back to me, then I'm correcting myself now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you saw neither the cafe, nor anything in the cafe or around the cafe?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You can't see the cafe itself from my window. But when it was hit, I could see the smoke. In front of the cafe, there are two trees, and the branches had been all broken by the shelling. You could see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you used these words. This was on page 16, at 16 hours and 13 minutes. You said: "From my window, I saw shells landing on Hotel Imperial, the Pile gate, and the Dubrovnik Cafe." Why weren't you precise then in your reply? Why didn't you say that you assumed that the Dubrovnik Cafe had been hit, that you didn't see what was there, who was there; that this was all your assumption? Why didn't you say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object. We just went through this. We just went through this. He said he saw the shell, he saw the explosion, the smoke, and then the next day he assumed it was the Cafe Dubrovnik, and the next day he saw it was in fact the Cafe Dubrovnik. We've just gone through that for five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I'm not sure what further point it is that you're wanting to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the point I'm trying to make is to show you that the witness did not see any of them. He saw the damage on the following day. But what was actually happening, and when it was happening, he couldn't see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, can I suggest that you've got it clear from the witness that he did not see the actual shell, or shells, landing on the cafe. It is not yet clear whether he saw anything directly about any other building at that time, such as the hotel. So if you want to pursue that, you may want to do that. Otherwise, I think it has become very clear from what you have put to him already that he did not actually see shells land on the cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will try to clarify this in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you say: "We were able to see shells flying." How can you see that? What does this look like? How did you see that happening?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we woke up that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you. I'm not asking you when you woke up or where you went. I'm simply asking you: You say: "We saw shells flying." What does this look like?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can tell by the sound. I may have used the word "saw" symbolically, but you can tell by the sound exactly how the shells were flying, and especially the incendiary shells. You can see those.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What is the difference between the sound of an incendiary and a non-incendiary projectile? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm no military expert, but I think the sound is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think you just said that you did draw a distinction. Maybe I misunderstood you. But, well, let this go. It doesn't matter. So whatever you say you saw, in fact you only heard it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Some things I saw and some things I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And some things you assumed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see the shells or did you hear them? I have to ask you again.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, I didn't see them, but I did hear them. I heard them very well. And I saw them on other occasions, and those were incendiary ones. But not on that day, because on that day I did not leave my cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What does an incendiary shell flying through the air look like? Can you describe it, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very shiny. You can see the flash of light. And if you saw the video footage of the boats that were hit and that burnt in the harbour on St. Nicholas's Day, then you would know what this flash of light looks like. I don't know how to explain it otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. That's sufficient. Did you go down to the cellar as soon as the shelling started?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the minute it started.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You didn't leave your cellar until 3.00 p.m. on that day?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us that you went down to the cellar when the shelling started, and you have just confirmed this. And then you said that at 3.00 p.m. you left the cellar. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me -- you said you didn't go, did you? And I wanted to confirm what you said. Maybe it was a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All right. That's what I wanted to hear. And whatever happened in the Old Town on that day, between 5.00 or 5.30 a.m. and 3.00 p.m., you didn't see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't see anything. Because we couldn't even stick our heads out to peep out of the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you couldn't see, for example, who was at Pile; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've answered that. If I didn't see anything, then how could I see someone at Pile.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, you're right. Nor could you have seen who was right next to the Old Town walls?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, but a while ago you asked me what I was able to see from the cellar. I was able to see the wall of the Franciscan monastery and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So nothing that was happening in or around the Old Town, from 5.00 a.m. to 3.00 p.m., you don't know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now show you a photograph. I ask you to assist me. Just a moment, please. Tell me: On that day, was the clock tower, the bell tower, hit?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On that day, was the Od Zigurate church targeted?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was St. Onofrio's fountain on that day?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was the damage made on that day on the city bell tower or clock tower?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I thought that was the date it had been hit. The cupola had been hit by a shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And what was the damage?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to tell you. The shell arrived from Zarkovica and from the side looking out to sea, the cupola was destroyed or damaged. Because on that day, over a thousand shells fell on the Old Town, and it's difficult to know when which building was hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And who told you about these thousand shells?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost every house in the Old Town was -- or 80 per cent of them were hit, and I saw that for myself afterwards. Almost every building on Prijeko had been hit. On Stradun itself, about 50. And then the Franciscan monastery. And I also read about it in the papers and the Institute for Cultural Heritage issued a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: How do you know that the city clock tower was hit from the sea side?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the cupola was damaged on the side overlooking the town harbour. So not from the side looking on to Lokrum, but the side looking on to the harbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, describe what the cupola looked like after it had been hit. Was any of it left?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it had -- it was kind of blown apart. It was jagged. I'm sure the Court will be able to see the photographs of the damage on the buildings that were hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher to show the witness a photograph now. [In English] Can you put it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me: Is this the city tower? Can you have a look?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see all of it, so I'm not sure. I think it is. You can't see all of it here, but just the upper part. But I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is this a picture taken before the attack and the damage, before the war?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just said: I'm not sure, because I can't see the clock. I've never been up there. And truth to tell, I'm not sure whether this actually is the city bell tower or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it says so underneath the photograph.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can write whatever you like down there, but I would like to see all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can help you and tell you that this is 01069833, a Prosecution exhibit, Exhibit number 35. If this assists the Chamber. And there is no doubt that this is in fact the city clock tower. So I'm asking you whether it was taken before or after 1991.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection [Previous translation continues]... Your Honour. Who is testifying here? He hasn't shown me the picture, so I haven't had a good chance to look at the picture. He's just shown it to the witness. That's number one. Number two, that's a single angle of a rectangular clock tower. He's not showing us all four sides or the total circumference of the clock tower. He can ask the witness, if the witness can't identify it, then he has to show it to another witness. He's trying to use it as a piece of evidence by a witness who can't even identify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you'll allow me, please. Your Honour, this is an excerpt from the Exhibit 35 of the Prosecution. I'm simply presenting something that exists in the Prosecutor's file of documents. This is a huge exhibit, as you probably know and it contains hundreds of pages. Therefore, I couldn't bring it with me, because that would be too incumbent. This is in fact the preliminary report of the Institute for the Cultural Protection of Dubrovnik, and as far as the bell tower is concerned, there were two photographs. One of them is this one that we are looking at now, and the other one I can show later. And I think my approach to this matter is quite correct, because this is something that we had seen before here. However, the witness is entitled to say that he doesn't know that; however, I believe that I am entitled to ask these kind of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You are certainly, Mr. Petrovic, able to put each of these photographs to the witness to see if he can identify what it shows and whether he can identify the damage that he's talking about in that photograph. Whether the damage will be visible in either of these photographs, I don't know. As Mr. Weiner points out, there are several sides to the building, and the photograph may not depict the side the witness is speaking about, if indeed it is a photograph of the tower that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the witness is speaking about. Do you have any concern about that, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I have no concern about him showing a photograph. I do have concerns about him showing a photograph, the witness saying that he doesn't recognise that, and then him testifying as to what it is. That's where my concern is. I also have a concern of him showing one angle of the bell tower, if it is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying, but please understand, Mr. Petrovic is relying on the exhibits that have been included in your brief of, he understands, the tower, and is wanting to ask questions about it. And I think we are spending a lot of time over some technical detail. Either the witness can identify the tower or not as the one he speaks of, and he will either be able to say that the damage he's speaking of is shown in the photograph or it isn't. And we will then be able to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that's what you're wanting to do, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grubisic, is this the eastern side of the town bell tower?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. As I said at the beginning, I had never gone upstairs. If I had had the whole picture, I could have known that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please give me back the photograph. This is the photograph as part of the Prosecutor's set of exhibits, and you can see the damage in the upper left corner that allegedly took place, according to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why, Mr. Grubisic, do you think that there's any point in your exaggerating this issue? Don't you think that in an already difficult and unhappy, unfortunate situation, there's no benefit to trying to prove something --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, if I could interrupt there. The witness has certainly not indicated that he sees in that photograph the damage that he has described, nor has he indicated that the damage shown in that photograph is damage that he can confirm occurred on the 6th of December. In those situations, you really can't put to him that his evidence in any way is exaggerating what actually occurred. You will have to lay a much more clear evidentiary foundation before it will be appropriate for such an observation to be made. Now, Mr. Weiner, does that deal with what you were wanting to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That is fine. I just -- I just want to comment that that is about the third or fourth time that this attorney has made what I would consider rude, condescending remarks to the witness, and I find it not acceptable here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner. If you would carry on, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I must reply to what Mr. Weiner just said. It is my right and it is my obligation to point out to the witness not speaking the truth if I feel that that is the case. There is nothing offending in that. I don't think why this is offensive, and what is the problem with that? This is my right. But I will not take more of your time, and I would like now to proceed to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, am I allowed to say something? I am also being offended by this gentleman implying that I'm not telling the truth. I have taken an oath, and I am telling the truth. Not a single word that I uttered was untrue. The only thing which I said at the beginning, I may be mistaken in some things about a date or a day when a certain building was hit, but I am just retelling of what I personally experienced. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Yesterday you mentioned Od Zigurate church. How was this church damaged?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it had been hit by a huge shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What kind of damage was inflicted?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
