utterances.text: The cupola and the whole roof was demolished. I apologise. I don't see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, there isn't. Just a second. Tell me: What kind of damage was inflicted on the cupola?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that it was damaged, but I didn't climb up there. It's being restored in the meantime. But what kind of damage was caused, you can only imagine how a shell can damage such things. I don't know how else to reply to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just to remind you of what the witness said yesterday about the church: "[In English] It had a little dome, and this was just blown apart."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I kindly ask the usher to show this photograph to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask the witness to say whether this is the Od Zigurate church?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please describe for me what you see in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that the roof is demolished, and I see other damage as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the cupola?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is that damaged or demolished also?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a very good photograph, but as I can see, the cupola is still standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So why did you tell us that it had been blown up?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what exact words I used, but I do know, and I'm telling you today, that it had been heavily damaged and that it was renovated in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't need the photograph any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you able, Mr. Petrovic, to identify what photograph that was that was shown to the witness? Is it a Prosecution exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the Prosecution Exhibit 35, and photograph is 01069209.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, I think you should have it marked for identification or offered as a piece of evidence. If he doesn't want to offer it, at least mark it for identification for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was thinking whether it would be appropriate, but due to the shortness of time, I wanted to do it this way, and I propose this to be included in the brief, and this would facilitate the work for all of us. So that's the photograph that I propose to be included and tendered into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Show the witness, I think it would be useful to mark them for identification, Mr. Petrovic. It will enable us all to know what it was at some later time, if it's relevant. But there were two photographs, in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is in fact the first photograph, and the one we've just seen would be the second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: All right. The first will be marked for identification first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The photograph bearing ERN number 01069833 will be D13, marked for identification. And photograph bearing ERN number 01069209 will be D14, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: May I ask to show this photograph to the witness as well, please. Here is the copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Grubisic, can you recognise from which location this photograph has been made, has been taken?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see in it St. Jacob, in the upper part. So it must have been taken from -- either from the walls or from the Jesuit church.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grubisic, this photograph shows the roof of the house on Celestina Medovica number 8. Do you know that house? If not, then it's all right.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The roof, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the photograph marked 01069192, attached to the preliminary report by the Institution for the Protection of Cultural Monuments, as part of the Exhibit P35 of the Prosecution, and is attached as an illustration of the text on the page 01069191, which speaks about damage on Celestina Medovica number 8. So can we please include these photographs for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I live on number 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The photograph will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D15, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'll just note for the record, Mr. Petrovic, that the reference to Prosecution Exhibit 35 is from, I think, the 65 ter list and not from this trial proceeding. Just so that it's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I apologise. I should have emphasised that this was Exhibit 35 from the 65 ter list, and my apologies for that. Could you please show this photograph to the witness, or rather, the drawing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark in this drawing where your house is located? If that's too difficult for you, then I'll give up. You have certain numbers here. The first street here is the Prijeko Street. So can you tell us near to which number your house was?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that my house was the first above the Prijeko Street, and so if you look at the Prijeko Street here, the first one would be my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to number 1?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I don't see number 1 here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you see number 14, at the bottom of the sketch?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you see number 1 right above it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is that where your house is?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm confused by this drawing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was confused by looking at this drawing on the screen. I do apologise for that. I would like to see the whole map. Only then could I be able to orient myself precisely; otherwise, this is kind of confusing for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On the left-hand side, is the Franciscan monastery. The Prijeko Street is horizontal and the first vertical street is yours. Is that helping?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know very well which my street is, and I pointed yesterday in the map exactly where my house was. However, I cannot work with this drawing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the sake of identification, this is also from 65 ter list. This is Exhibit number 10969188. Could you please mark it for identification so that we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is the point of marking this for identification, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will explain what it's all about. So this is a very good layout, or a map, and based on this map, individual identification of the damage were established on the street. So on the basis of this map, individual analyses had been made about the degree of damage. I believe that the witness would be able to recognise that his house was there. However, if he's not able to do that, I will not insist on this, and I propose that we proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. As the witness can't identify it, it shouldn't be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully agree.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a very bad picture. If I had a good map in front of me, however, it is very difficult for me to identify from this kind of picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, I have the same problem. But as I understand, you are not able to identify your house, so let us go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me something about the damage on your house inflicted on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only one shell hit the roof of my house. There was no other damage. There were also some fragments that landed on the Franciscan monastery, and they had broken windows on my studies and on the stone. You can see the damage caused by the fragment. Some four metres of the floor was blown up -- of the roof - sorry - was blown up by a grenade. However, a friend of mine repaired the roof, in order to stop the rain from coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Has anyone photographed the damage on your house inflicted on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you open the door to your house for anyone to come in and look at what the damage was?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said no, because we had already repaired the roof two or three days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So no one from the Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments marked your house or recorded your house as having been damaged in the events of 6th December?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe they did, but not at that time. That would have been much later. As I said, it was repaired, but the roof was part of the overall renovation, and it has been renovated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So at 3.00 p.m. on December the 6th, no one came to your house to see the damage?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What date?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, 6th of December, 1991, at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that, but I don't know. I think not, at that time. I think. Because, as I said, we had already repaired it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what the size was of the opening on your roof?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About three or four square metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If I told you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bear with me for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Was there any other damage on your building, apart from the hole in the roof? What about the walls?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The plaster on the walls?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Any cracks?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please: The Domino church, or All Saints Church, what was the damage on the roof of that church?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard for me to say, because I never climbed up onto the roof. But we had to replace the entire roof, because later on, on the 30th or on the 1st of June, 1992, there was more damage, so we had to repair the entire roof. And friends helped us stop the holes. And I wouldn't be able to answer your question, because I couldn't climb up and I couldn't see from below.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me exactly what damage was inflicted on the 6th of December and which damage in May or June 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The roof was hit on the 6th, right above the balustrade, as I said, and the ceiling had been pierced, and the plaster fell on the balustrade. In front of the church, a shell had landed, which had shattered the stairs, both windows, and the rose window above the portal. In late May or early June, a shell landed below the window. There were two round windows at the sides of the altar, and the one facing the Stradun, on the north, that's where an enormous projectile hit the church, underneath the window. It did not pierce through. But four or five square metres of stone inside, near the entrance to the sacristy, and the sanctuary where the altar is, four or five square metres of stones fell down onto the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So what damage occurred, when?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. What happened to the rose window?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rose window was so badly damaged that we had to replace it and put in a new one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was it blown up, shattered?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The right-hand window was blown up, right to the right when you're leaving the church, toward the Od Puca Street. That was completely destroyed. The rose window, however, had been partly hit but the damage was such that it had to be replaced altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What about the carving of the rose window?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was only the glass shattered, or the entire window?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that all the glass was shattered, but the wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I was referring to the stone carvings.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The stone was not destroyed. It may have been hit by a few pieces of shrapnel. I don't think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was your house hit at any other time except on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure your house was not hit on the 12th of November?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: From whom did you hear that Sofronije Jeremic was to arrive in the city of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it on the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What exactly did you hear on the radio?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you right now, but it was that he was to land in the city harbour, either for negotiations or, if I'm not mistaken, some kind of international military delegation had arrived. And he arrived on the same occasion, and that is why we took the liberty of coming seeing him in the city harbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you know when he was to arrive, at what time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. But when they said that he had arrived, that was when I went to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why he came to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that I don't, but I assumed that because an international military delegation had arrived, that was the reason. But I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What kind of uniform was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't wearing a uniform. He was wearing very elegant clothes. I found him on the boat. And he was drinking Bevanda, a mixture of wine and water, which was in a glass in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And what you're talk about was described in a newspaper article, if I'm not wrong?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mato Jerinic, a journalist from our area, wrote about it, I think in Slobodna Dalmacija.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What did you do with this article?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I kept the cutting as a memento.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you give it to anyone?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who did you give it to?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When The Hague investigators came to interview me, when we got to this topic, I gave them a copy of that article.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did they show you the article again when you arrived in The Hague now?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me briefly, please: How did you go to Konavle, and who gave you approval to go there on Christmas of that year?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The late Don Vlado Puce was in Konavle. He was the only priest who had remained there. And he was taking care of all the parishes. He requested assistance at Christmastime. And in Dubrovnik, we had to ask for permission, but it was the late Don Vlado who went to ask for it, and I think that this was in Cavtat. It was called the command or something like that. And then we took the boat that for a while ran between Dubrovnik and Cavtat, and we went to Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And were you able to hold services in the churches in Konavle?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just short.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Father Grubisic, they asked you about Captain Jeremic's visit. Did Captain Jeremic complain to you or ask you about any Croatian troops or soldiers in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did Captain Jeremic indicate any concern about any Croatian troops or soldiers being in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You told us that you complained to Captain Jeremic about the different problems. Did he offer any response, something in relation to orders?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He only said that he was carrying out orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he said he was carrying out orders in relation to what? That was his response in relation to which complaints?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said to him: "Sir, what kind of opinion can we have of you when we hear on the radio that you ordered food to be thrown into the sea, milk, batteries, all the things we who are under siege need?" He just kept repeating: "I'm only carrying out orders."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I would like you to look at the screen. I want to show you a photograph on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could the usher please assist the witness for one moment. Is it on the screen, sir? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you look at that building. Do you recognise that, the building -- the hole, the large hole in the cupola?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I recognise it, because you can see the green men who hit the clock [as interpreted], the bell. This is the city bell tower cupola. I didn't recognise the other photograph, but I do recognise this one. And you can see the hole on the cupola. I think this was on the 12th. I said at the beginning that it's very difficult for me to give a precise date for every hit, because it's been 13 or 14 years ago. But yes, this is the city bell tower. This is a very clear picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And on the cupola, is that the damage that you saw to the bell tower?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can we have an identification for this photograph? What sort of document it is, where it's from, its number, its marking, anything about this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if he gives me a moment. We were not prepared to offer this photo today, but I'd like to give the ERN number and offer it tomorrow. This is one of the photographs, one of the many photographs that had been provided to Defence, and the ERN number is -- it doesn't have an ERN number. It was on the disk provided to the Defence on the 15th of December. I was hoping to offer it tomorrow, based -- since it's almost 5.15, and -- but if we could -- the reference is -- on the Sanction list is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this being displayed from the disk?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. No. It's being displayed through Sanction, which is the internal system of the Office of the Prosecutor. Copies are on the way right now. We should have them in a few moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And they are from a disk provided on the 15th of December last --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, maybe we could even remedy some of this problem. In some of the other cases, similar to the Prosecution notifying the Defence in advance as to new documents it's planning to use, they also require the Defence to notify the Prosecution as to documents it's planning -- new documents it's planning to use. In this manner, we've already seen the document, so we have an idea what they're showing the witness; and number two, we also have the chance, like in this situation, to have information available to respond, as opposing to trying to e-mail upstairs and trying to get a quick copy of a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sure that will be borne in mind by Mr. Petrovic and Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, whenever possible, yes, of course. But there are some situations where the course of a testimony prevents this. However, whenever we are able to do so, we will notify our learned friends as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something? May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, Don Grubisic, it might be quicker and better if you just left it to Mr. Weiner to ask you the questions at this stage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And just the final question, sir, the final area of questions. Were you in your shelter, in your home in that cellar which you were using as a shelter, on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not every day, but whenever there was an alert or shelling taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And sir, during the evenings, did you stay in the shelter, or we'll call it the cellar? In your cellar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And after these alerts would end, what would you do?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would return to the flat and continue as usual, do our business about the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And on those days when there was no shelling or no alerts, did you walk around the town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you ever see any Croatian troops or anyone firing from outside of the town on those days?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: At this moment, Your Honour, I'd like to offer copies of this photograph which the witness has identified as the bell tower, with the large hole in the cupola.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If the document could be brought forward to the court officer, please, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That document will be received, then, into evidence, that photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P31.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Don Grubisic, may I thank you very much for your attendance and your assistance. That concludes your evidence. You are now free to return to your home and to the work that you needed to do this coming weekend.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I wanted to say something, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It would be more appropriate if you did not, leaving it to counsel to decide what matters you should speak about or what you shouldn't. I trust you'll understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You may leave now, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It appears clear that we will not be able to proceed with any further witness this afternoon. So the next witness will be -- or the next, Mr. Samardzic, will continue in the morning when we resume, at 9.00. Could I ask Mr. Rodic or Mr. Petrovic whether any consideration has yet been given to the Prosecution's motion for protective measures in the case of one witness, that was filed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have received this motion yesterday, and regardless of the usual deadline for responding, we are going to do that in an appropriate manner, and we shall be able to respond to this brief on Monday. If we should do it sooner, we shall make additional effort to comply; however, we were not able to do that more quickly because the usual time frame is two weeks. However, we shall do our best and respond on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I wonder, Mr. Petrovic, whether it might be possible simply to respond orally tomorrow. Given the time constraints, it would be I think possible for you to evaluate it. Can I say that given that there is in place a standing order for protection measures, it really is only, as I see it, the first of the proposals that is alive. The rest appears to be covered by the standing order. And I think it should not take very long at all for a view to be formed about the first of the proposed orders, and an oral indication in the morning would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if that is in order, we will be able to state our views towards the end of tomorrow's working day, if you approve, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes. Could I indicate to Ms. Somers that it seemed to us that on a matter such as this, it might be practical to approach the matter orally rather than for you to go to the trouble of a written submission.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. If this is a standing directive of the Chamber, I'd be very grateful. I'm trying to avoid written submissions where possible. And the only issue would be of course on these matters we'd have to do it in closed or private session. And I would certainly appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. As long as you could let the Defence counsel know that you have in mind to raise a matter, and then I think it will cut down the amount of work for both parties if we avoid unnecessary written documents over matters as straightforward as this. There will be other matters, of course, where written documents will be necessary, to ensure that proper consideration is given, but this appears not to be of complexity, and an oral submission on both sides would be adequate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of Mr. Strugar shares your views. I would only ask you that, if possible, we should allocate a few minutes to present arguments concerning the submission regarding the extension of deadlines for expert witnesses. I think that you have issued order in that respect, that we should try and find five or ten minutes during this week. So maybe it could be convenient to do that tomorrow, of course, if you would allow that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. We will adjourn now until tomorrow morning. Could I remind everybody that we will be in Courtroom I tomorrow, rather than this courtroom, at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 23rd day of January 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.25 p.m.,
